segments.text:
- The comment introduces three kernels that the version bwx11 added. Each one is the asmread loop with 64, 96 or 128 `nop` instructions between the 8 loads and the `add` of the read address.
- "Round 4" is the work step of 2026-11-15 that produced bwx11 (line 36). It is not a round of `--rounds`.
- The three kernels stand after all older kernels in the source. The comment gives the reason: the older kernels keep their place in the binary.
- Each function saves d8 to d15 before its loop, as `k_asmread` does. So it gets the pad of asmread, and its loop starts at 20 modulo 64 [Ref1].
- Of these three kernels the whole-chip test runs only `read_nop96`.
segments.heading: Kernels added by bwx11: `read_nop64`, `read_nop96`, `read_nop128`

segments.text:
- Default pads of the three kernels. Each name gets the value of `PAD_asmread`, unless the build sets another value with a `-D` option.
- `PAD_asmread` is 0 (line 214). The CRB build has no `-D` option [Ref2].
- So `PLACE` (line 163) lets each of the three functions start on a 64 B boundary.
Creates the kernel `read_nop64` from the macro `DEF_ASMREAD`: the asmread loop with 64 `nop` instructions per 256 B. The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 does not run it.

- This line creates the function `k_read_nop96` from the macro `DEF_ASMREAD` (lines 616 to 641) with the nop count 96. Part L and control I run it at position 2 of the sequence. Part C does not run it [Ref4].
- The loop is assembler text that gcc does not change. gcc only chooses the registers: x0 holds the read address and x1 holds the end address [Ref1].
- One loop pass reads 256 B with 8 `ldp` instructions. Each one loads 32 B into two of the registers q0 to q15, at the byte offsets 0, 32, 64, ... 224. So each byte is read once. Nothing uses the loaded values.
- After the 8 loads the text `.rept 96`, `nop`, `.endr` tells the assembler to write the `nop` instruction 96 times. Then `add` moves the read address forward by 256 B. `cmp` compares it with the end address. `b.lo 1b` branches back to the first `ldp` while the read address is below the end address.
- Listing [Ref1]: one loop pass is 8 `ldp`, 96 `nop`, `add x0, x0, #0x100`, `cmp x0, x1` and `b.cc`. That is 107 instructions (428 B of code) per 256 B of data. The listing prints the branch as `b.cc` and names `b.lo` as another name of the same instruction. The function starts at address 0x57c0 (0 modulo 64) and the loop at 0x57d4 (20 modulo 64), the loop offset of `k_asmread`.
- Outside the loop, once per call: 4 `stp` instructions save d8 to d15 on the stack, one `add` computes the end address, 4 `ldp` instructions load d8 to d15 back, and `ret` returns. In a timed interval of the test one call covers one 2 MiB chunk. That is 8192 loop passes.
segments.heading: Kernel `read_nop96`: function `k_read_nop96`

segments.text: Creates the kernel `read_nop128`: the asmread loop with 128 `nop` instructions per 256 B. The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 does not run it.

- `PAD_after_kernels11` gets the value of `PAD_after_kernels`: 24 (line 1037).
- `PLACE(after_kernels11)` pads the code up to a 64 B boundary and then adds 24 bytes of value 0.
- In bwx11 this pad set the start address of the function that follows the kernels. In bwx12 more kernels follow here, and the pad of line 1449 sets that start address.
- Lines 1076 and 1077 are markers. The text that bwx11 added ends here, and the text that bwx12 added starts.
segments.heading: Second pad after the kernels

segments.text:
- The comment gives the placement rule for the 26 kernels that bwx12 added. "Round 5" is the work step of 2026-11-15 that produced bwx12 (line 3).
- Aim: the loop of each new kernel starts at a planned address modulo 64. That is 20 B for a read kernel (the loop offset of asmread), 40 B for a write kernel (the loop offset of asmwrite) and 52 B for a copy kernel (the loop offset of asmcopy).
- Rule: pad = (LOOP - HEAD) modulo 64. LOOP is the planned loop offset. HEAD is the number of bytes of code between the function start and the loop start.
- The listing of the CRB binary shows the planned loop offset for each of the 26 kernels [Ref1].
- Of these 26 kernels the whole-chip test runs only `read_nop256`.
segments.heading: Kernels added by bwx12: where each loop starts

segments.text: `LOOP_read12` is the planned loop offset of the new read kernels: 20 B. The three `HEAD` values are the bytes of code before the loop: 52 B for the `read_dadd` kernels, 84 B for `read_iadd16` and 4 B for the `read_sp` kernels. The listing of the CRB binary shows these three distances [Ref1].
Default pads of 8 new `read_nop` kernels: the value of `PAD_asmread`, 0. The whole-chip test runs none of these 8 kernels.
`PAD_read_nop256` gets the same value 0. So `k_read_nop256`, a kernel of the test, starts on a 64 B boundary. The listing shows the start address 0x6cc0. That is 0 modulo 64 [Ref1].

Default pads of 10 kernels that the whole-chip test does not run. `PADOF(loop, head)` (line 164) computes (loop - head) modulo 64. The results are 32 B for the four `read_dadd` kernels, 0 B for `read_iadd16` and 16 B for the five `read_sp` kernels.

Default pads of 7 more kernels that the whole-chip test does not run. `read_1pl_nop96` takes the pad of `read_1pl` (16 B). The four `write_nop` kernels take the pad of `asmwrite` (32 B). The two `copy_nop` kernels take the pad of `asmcopy` (32 B).

Creates 8 kernels from the macro `DEF_ASMREAD` (lines 616 to 641): the asmread loop with 48, 56, 72, 80, 88, 112, 160 or 192 `nop` instructions per 256 B. The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 runs none of them.

- This line creates the function `k_read_nop256` from the macro `DEF_ASMREAD` (lines 616 to 641) with the nop count 256. Part L and control I run it at position 3 of the sequence. Part C does not run it [Ref4].
- The loop is the loop of `k_read_nop96` (line 1063) with 256 `nop` instructions in place of 96. gcc does not change the assembler text. x0 holds the read address and x1 holds the end address [Ref1].
- One loop pass reads 256 B with 8 `ldp` instructions of 32 B each, at the byte offsets 0, 32, 64, ... 224. So each byte is read once. Nothing uses the loaded values.
- Listing [Ref1]: one loop pass is 8 `ldp`, 256 `nop`, `add x0, x0, #0x100`, `cmp x0, x1` and the branch `b.cc` (another name of `b.lo`). That is 267 instructions (1068 B of code) per 256 B of data.
- The function starts at address 0x6cc0 (0 modulo 64). The loop starts at 0x6cd4 (20 modulo 64), the loop offset of `k_asmread`.
- Outside the loop, once per call: 4 `stp` instructions save d8 to d15 on the stack, one `add` computes the end address, 4 `ldp` instructions load d8 to d15 back, and `ret` returns. In a timed interval of the test one call covers one 2 MiB chunk. That is 8192 loop passes.
segments.heading: Kernel `read_nop256`: function `k_read_nop256`

segments.text: `#if defined(__aarch64__)`: lines 1202 to 1405 are compiled only for AArch64. The CRB binary holds this branch. Proof: the listing holds `k_read_dadd2` with the `movi` and vector `add` instructions of line 1273 [Ref1]. The whole-chip test runs no kernel of this branch.
segments.heading: AArch64 branch of the other bwx12 kernels

segments.text:
- The comment describes the macro `DEF_READ_ADD` and the five kernels that are built from it. Each one is the asmread loop with vector adds between the 8 loads and the `add` of the read address.
- In a `read_daddK` kernel each of the K adds takes one register that the loads of the same loop pass filled. The other input is one of the sum registers v16 to v23.
- In `read_iadd16` the 16 adds take the constants in v24 to v31 and no loaded register.
- The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 runs none of them.
segments.heading: `read_dadd` kernels and `read_iadd16`: not run by the test

segments.text:
Three pieces of assembler text for the macro below.
- `ACC_ZERO`: 8 `movi` instructions that set the sum registers v16 to v23 to 0. `movi` is the Arm instruction that writes a constant into a vector register.
- `CONST_ONE`: 8 `movi` instructions that set each 32-bit part of v24 to v31 to 1.
- `VADD(a, b)`: the instruction `add va.2d, va.2d, vb.2d`. It adds register b to register a as two 64-bit numbers.

- The macro `DEF_READ_ADD(name, init, adds)` creates the function `k_<name>`.
- The text `init` runs once per call, before the loop label `1:`.
- One loop pass is the 8 `ldp` loads of asmread, then the text `adds`, then `add`, `cmp` and `b.lo`.
- The last part of the `asm` statement names v0 to v31 as registers that the text changes. So gcc saves d8 to d15 once per call, as in `k_asmread` [Ref1].

Creates five kernels. `read_dadd2`, `read_dadd4`, `read_dadd8` and `read_dadd16` have 2, 4, 8 and 16 vector adds of loaded registers per 256 B. `read_iadd16` has 16 vector adds of constants per 256 B. The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 runs none of them.

- The macro `DEF_READ_SP(name, nops)` creates a kernel whose loop pass reads 128 B with 4 `ldp` instructions. Then follow `nops` `nop` instructions, `add`, `cmp` and `b.lo`.
- The `asm` statement names only v0 to v7 as changed. So gcc saves no register in these functions [Ref1].
- Lines 1306 to 1310 create `read_sp24`, `read_sp32`, `read_sp40`, `read_sp48` and `read_sp56` with 24, 32, 40, 48 and 56 `nop`.
- The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 runs none of them.
segments.heading: `read_sp` kernels: not run by the test

segments.text:
- The kernel `read_1pl_nop96`: the loop of `k_read_1pl` (line 988) with 96 `nop` instructions after the four loads.
- One loop pass walks 256 B and loads 16 B at the start of each 64 B line with `ldr`.
- The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 does not run it. The test runs `read_1pl`. That kernel has no `nop`.
segments.heading: Function `k_read_1pl_nop96`: not run by the test

segments.text:
- The macro `DEF_ASMWRITE_NOP(name, nops)` creates a write kernel: the loop of `DEF_ASMWRITE` (line 671) with `nops` `nop` instructions after the 8 `stp` stores. One `stp` stores 32 B: the 16-byte register q0 twice.
- Lines 1361 to 1364 create `write_nop32`, `write_nop96`, `write_nop128` and `write_nop256`.
- The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 runs none of them.
segments.heading: `write_nop` kernels: not run by the test

segments.text: The macro `DEF_ASMCOPY_NOP(name, nops)` creates a copy kernel: the loop of `DEF_ASMCOPY` (line 698) with `nops` `nop` instructions after the 8 `stp` stores and before the two `add`. One loop pass loads 256 B from the source buffer with 8 `ldp` and stores them to the destination buffer with 8 `stp`.
segments.heading: `copy_nop` kernels: not run by the test

segments.text: Creates the copy kernels `copy_nop96` and `copy_nop192`. The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 runs neither of them.

- `#else` branch of the `#if` of line 1201. It is compiled only when the target is not AArch64.
- In that case each kernel of lines 1273 to 1405 becomes a plain C loop: the stand-in macro of its original, or the loop of lines 1427 to 1430 for `read_1pl_nop96`.
- The CRB binary does not hold this branch. Line 2 of every csv file of the test says `kernels=aarch64` [Ref5].
- Line 1438 ends the `#if`.
segments.heading: Stand-ins of the bwx12 kernels: not in the CRB binary

segments.text:
- `PAD_after_kernels12` gets the value of `PAD_after_kernels`: 24 (line 1037).
- `PLACE(after_kernels12)` pads the code up to a 64 B boundary and then adds 24 bytes of value 0. So the function after it starts at 24 modulo 64.
- That function is `call` (line 1491). The build record of CRB gives `call=24` for the start of `call` modulo 64 [Ref2].
- The comment gives the aim: the code after the kernels keeps the placement modulo 64 that it has in bwx11, bwx10 and bwx8.
- Line 1450 is a marker: the text that bwx12 added ends here.
segments.heading: Third pad: the start address of `call`

segments.text:
- Each entry is one `struct kdef`: the name of a kernel, its type and a pointer to its function.
- The name is the word that `--seq` accepts. `parse_seq` (line 1750) compares each word of `--seq` with the names and stores the index of the entry that matches.
- The type is one of `T_READ`, `T_WRITE`, `T_COPY` and `T_OLDREAD` (line 253). It tells `call` which arguments the function takes.
- The macro `K(name, type)` writes one entry. `K(read, T_READ)` becomes `{ "read", T_READ, (void (*)(void))k_read }`.
- The cast stores every function pointer as one common pointer type. `call` casts it back to the real type before it calls the function.
- For each interval the worker takes the entry of the kernel from this table (line 1658) and passes it to `call`.
segments.heading: The kernel table `kernels[]`

segments.text:
The 21 kernels that the older version bwx8 already had (entries 0 to 20). Three of them are kernels of the test:
- `read` is entry 0, type `T_READ`: the new read kernel.
- `asmread` is entry 3, type `T_READ`.
- `oldread` is entry 6, type `T_OLDREAD`: the old read kernel.
The 5 kernels that bwx10 added (entries 21 to 25). `read_1pl`, a kernel of the test, is entry 25 with the type `T_READ`.
The 3 kernels that bwx11 added (entries 26 to 28). `read_nop96`, a kernel of the test, is entry 27 with the type `T_READ`.
The 26 kernels that bwx12 added (entries 29 to 54). `read_nop256`, a kernel of the test, is entry 37 with the type `T_READ`. The test runs no other kernel of these lines.

`K_COUNT` is the number of entries: the size of the table divided by the size of one entry. It is 55. The `--seq` lists of the test name 6 of the 55 kernels. The worker calls `k_write` directly for the first touch (line 1646), not through the table.

- `kd` is the table entry of the kernel. `t` is the record of the calling thread. `off` and `len` give the range in bytes. `v` is the value that a write kernel stores. `sink` points to the variable that takes the sum of an old read kernel.
- The worker calls this function once per interval for the warm-up pass (line 1669), and once for each 2 MiB chunk of the timed loop (line 1695).
- In the timed loop the function runs between the clock reads `t0` and `t1`. So its own instructions are part of the timed interval, once per 2 MiB chunk.
segments.heading: Function `call`: run one kernel on one range of a buffer

segments.text:
- `a` is the address of the first word of the range. `t->a` points to 8-byte words. So `off / 8` words are `off` bytes.
- `n` is the length of the range in 8-byte words. One 2 MiB chunk gives 262144 words. The warm-up pass over the whole 256 MiB buffer gives 33554432 words.

`switch` chooses the form of the call by the type of the kernel. Case `T_READ`: the pointer is cast to the type `read_fn` (line 254), and the kernel is called with the address and the word count. It returns nothing. The kernels `read`, `asmread`, `read_nop96`, `read_nop256` and `read_1pl` of the test take this path.

- Case `T_OLDREAD`: the kernel returns its sum, and this line stores the sum to `*sink`.
- `sink` points to a `volatile` variable on the stack of the worker (line 1635). So the compiler must keep the store and must compute the sum. The listing of `k_oldread` holds the adds [Ref1].
- The kernel `oldread` of the test takes this path.
- This path has one 8-byte store per call that the `T_READ` path does not have. In the timed loop that is one store per 2 MiB chunk.

- Case `T_WRITE` passes the value `v` to a write kernel.
- Case `T_COPY` calls a copy kernel that reads buffer `a` and writes buffer `b`.
- No kernel in a `--seq` list of the test has one of these two types. So the two cases do not run in the test.
- The function returns no value.

- For each of the `n` buffer addresses in `buf` the function looks for the mapping of that buffer in the Linux file `/proc/self/smaps`. It writes two values to `pg`: the size of the mapping and the part of it on 2 MiB pages, both in kB.
- In the test `main` calls it with 240 entries, two per thread (line 3111). The 120 entries of the second buffers are NULL, and the function skips them.
- `main` calls it before the first interval and after each interval. During the call all workers wait at the barrier (line 1653 or line 1731). So the call is not timed.
segments.heading: Function `read_smaps`: page state of the buffers

segments.text: `len` is the buffer length from `buf_len` (line 426): 268435456 bytes in the test. `cur` is the index of the buffer whose mapping the loop below is reading, or -1 for no buffer. The loop of lines 1520 to 1521 sets both values of every entry to -1. The value -1 means "not found".

Opens `/proc/self/smaps` for reading. The file lists every memory mapping of the process. So it holds the buffers of all threads. When the file does not open, the function returns and all values stay -1.

- The loop reads the file line by line.
- `sscanf` returns 3 when the line starts with `start-end` (two hexadecimal addresses) and a word after them. Such a line is the first line of a mapping.
- At such a line `cur` is first set back to -1 (line 1529). Then the inner loop compares the mapping with every buffer. A buffer matches when the mapping starts at the buffer address and ends exactly `len` bytes after it. Then `cur` becomes the index of that buffer.
- When no buffer matches, `cur` is -1. So the lines of that mapping store nothing, and they cannot change the values of a buffer that was read before.
- The comment of `alloc_buf` (lines 431 to 433) gives the reason for the exact test. No-access ranges stand before and after each buffer. So Linux lists the buffer as one mapping of its own.

- Every other line belongs to the mapping whose first line was read last. The branch runs only when that mapping is a buffer (`cur >= 0`).
- The first `sscanf` stores a number only when the line starts with `Size:`. The number is the size of the mapping in kB and goes to `kb_total`.
- The second `sscanf` stores a number only when the line starts with `AnonHugePages:`. The number is the part of the mapping on 2 MiB pages in kB and goes to `kb_huge`.
- All other lines store nothing.

Closes the file. If one of the two values of an entry is still below 0, both are set to -1. `print_p` (line 1570) prints a value below 0 as `NA`. In the test every P row holds 262144 kB for both values [Ref5].

Reads four counters from the Linux file `/proc/vmstat` into `vm[0]` to `vm[3]`, in the order of the names in line 1547. They count for the whole system, not for one buffer. They become the last four columns of every P row.
segments.heading: Function `read_vmstat`: four counters of the whole system

segments.text: Sets the four values to -1. The value -1 means "not found". Then opens the file. When it does not open, the function returns with the four values at -1.

- Each line of the file holds a name and a number. `fscanf` reads one such pair per loop pass.
- When the name equals one of the four names, the number goes to the matching place in `vm`.
- The loop ends when `fscanf` finds no further pair, for example at the end of the file.
- In the test `main` calls this function once before the first interval and once after each interval (line 3112). It is not timed.
